rationale: The running-clock experiment executed in a clean copy (e7cdea5042e54182b277e185ae576ea8, completed, exit 0) with all eighteen comparisons complete and evaluated: after ten rounds of ticks to every node the leader was still node 1 in StateLeader at term 1, the re-added node was still a voter, and the context-free invocation was still pending, so the logical clock itself neither triggers an election nor releases the held proposal; the invocation was admitted only after the forced leader change, 4637 ms after it was issued, and its payload was then committed. This update attributes that retained interpretation, records the running-clock observation as durable knowledge with receipt indices, retires the no-ticks limitation, and marks the investigation's question answered.

investigations.discriminator: Drive a real three-node Node-API cluster (config {1,2,3}, leader 1) through a committed removal and re-addition of node 3, then invoke Propose and ProposeConfChange on node 3 (bounded contexts, a context-free context, a retry cycle, and with the logical clock running) and Propose on never-removed node 2 with the same leader, recording for each whether it returns, with which error, and whether its payload reaches any node's committed entries; finally force a leader change and observe both a new invocation and the still-pending context-free invocation.

knowledge.statement: Advancing the logical clock does not release a proposal held by the disarmed gate. In the retained run, ten rounds of Tick to every node (with message delivery between rounds, so leader heartbeats kept flowing and no election was triggered) left node 1 in StateLeader at term 1, the re-added node 3 a voter seeing leader 1, and the context-free invocation still pending; that invocation was admitted only after a forced campaign installed node 2 as leader at term 2, 4637 ms after it was issued, and its payload was committed on all three nodes.
knowledge.conditions: Async Node API, three nodes (1,2,3) in one process with ElectionTick 10 and HeartbeatTick 1; node 3 removed by joint-implicit configuration change and re-added by a committed change with leader 1 unchanged; ticks delivered in ten rounds with delivery between rounds; no message loss.

interpretations.rationale: Seven retained executions agree. In e7cdea5042e54182b277e185ae576ea8 the witness admission chain is ctx, reapplied, removal and admit (indices 5, 4, 2, 6) and all eighteen comparisons are complete and evaluated: witness pending at 1201 ms (index 7) with release only at the caller's deadline (index 8) and no committed payload (index 9); the context-free invocation pending at 2001 ms (index 11) and uncommitted (index 12); after ten rounds of ticks to every node with delivery between rounds, leader 1 still in StateLeader at term 1, node 3 still a voter seeing leader 1, and the invocation still pending (index 13); the configuration proposal pending at its window with nothing applied (indices 15, 16); the never-removed member returning immediately and committing (indices 18, 19); both retries pending (indices 21, 26) while member proposals committed in those intervals (indices 24, 29); the post-leader-change invocation returning immediately and committing (indices 32, 33); and the context-free invocation admitted 4637 ms after it was issued once the gate was re-armed (index 34) with its payload committed on all three nodes (index 35). Source account: the run loop's gate variable is assigned only at node.go:374 (leader observed), 377 (no leader) and 426 (local member removed) and used as the receive case at node.go:386, so all MsgProp traffic of the member stays pending on the non-nil n.propc channel (node.go:525) until an observed leader change re-arms the receive side; the removal guard fires because applying the removal conf change leaves the local node without a Progress entry (node.go:401-412). The snapshot's own expectation (node_test.go:352-385) scopes intended blocking to a node that does not know the current leader, which is not this case. Controls exclude cluster-wide stalls, a broken state machine, the running clock as the releasing cause, and a single removal form.

knowledge.assertion: propc is armed only on observed leader change and is left nil after a re-admission
the caller sends on n.propc and stays pending while the run loop's gate variable is disarmed; a later observed leader change admits the pending request
the raft state machine returns ErrProposalDropped for a removed leader instead of blocking
intended blocking is scoped to the unknown-leader case and acceptance is expected once a leader is known; re-addition is untested
a configuration change proposed through the re-added voter was held pending and was not applied by any node
a joint-consensus removal with automatic leave leads to the same held-proposal effect after the member is re-added
advancing the logical clock left the held invocation pending with leader 1 still in StateLeader; admission came only with the leader change

counterevidence: node.go:407-411 acknowledges the gate as improvised ('propc is reset when the leader changes ... This isn't very sound and likely has bugs'); this explains the dependence on leader changes but is neither a calling restriction nor a protection, and no other re-arm path exists in the snapshot.

node_test.go:352-385 shows that not returning is intended for a node that does not know the current leader. That expectation does not cover the witnessed case, and the same test expects acceptance once a leader is known.

No request is lost: held invocations are admitted unmodified once the gate is re-armed (indices 34, 35), so the harm is an unbounded wait without an error signal rather than data loss or a protocol safety violation.
The same runs contain successful paths (indices 18, 19, 24, 29, 33), showing proposals are neither generally dropped nor generally blocked.
limitations: Comparison outcomes for the earliest receipt were 'unknown' because that harness gave the three operations' result events the same names; its decisive events are complete and match the successor receipts, which have complete holds.

Scope is the async Node API path (node.run loop) in this snapshot; RawNode.Propose and RawNode.ProposeConfChange have no such gate. Message delivery is reliable in the harness, so no message-loss characterization is claimed.

Two removal forms were executed (simple ConfChange and joint-implicit with automatic leave). Transitions that keep the member in a half of the configuration were not executed; the guard reads the local Progress entry, so they are expected not to disarm the gate, but that expectation is source-derived only.

The executed revision's prefix prose for one earlier experiment described a simple removal while its fixed harness performed the joint one; the harness artifacts and this record describe the executed behaviour.

The configuration-proposal case was executed with a single proposal (add node 9) and a single window; it establishes that the administrative entry point is affected, not a distribution over configuration-change kinds.

The ticks were delivered in ten rounds with delivery between rounds, which is enough to advance both timeouts without triggering an election in this harness; other tick schedules (for example ticks that outpace message delivery) were not executed, and no claim is made about a partition-like case in which the member hears no leader traffic.

All seven build the same configuration {1,2,3} from the same storage ConfState, elect leader 1 at term 1, remove node 3 by committed configuration change (simple, then joint-implicit) and re-add it, run the same invocation cases, deadlines and windows, and force the same campaign of node 2 into term 2; the successors add naming, retry/progress cases, the context-free case, the post-re-arm observations, the configuration proposal and the running clock. Witnesses agree field for field (witness 7/8/9 in all seven; context-free 11/12; configuration proposal 14/15; control 17/18; progress commits; repair 31/32 or 32/33), so the effect is a property of the scenario rather than of one run, removal form or clock state.
